summary: Specifies the format and content of data escrow deposits, primarily for domain name registries, in a way that is independent of the objects being escrowed. This lets a registry keep a safe copy of its data. It is standards-track.

plainLanguage.summary: Companies that run domain names keep a backup copy of their records with a trusted third party. This document defines how that backup is organized so it can be read if something goes wrong.

questions: what format are domain registry escrow deposits
how to rebuild a registry from escrow deposits
difference between full incremental differential deposits
subtitle: A standardized format for domain registries to back up their data safely.

tldr.problem: Domain name registries need a way to regularly deposit their data with a trusted third party to ensure continuity if the registry fails or becomes unable to operate.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8909 defines a standardized XML format for Registry Data Escrow deposits, allowing registries to submit complete (Full), incremental, or differential snapshots of their data in a consistent way.
tldr.outcome: Registries can safely back up their records, and in case of catastrophic failure, a third-party escrow agent or backup registry can restore the service using the deposited data.

today: RFC 8909 is an Internet Standard that defines the format for domain registry data escrow. It has not been obsoleted and remains the current specification for this purpose. Registries for gTLDs and many ccTLDs are required by their agreements to use this format for data escrow deposits.

sections.title: Introduction to Registry Data Escrow
sections.content:
Registry Data Escrow (RDE) is the process by which a domain name registry periodically deposits its records to a third party called an escrow agent. These deposits contain the minimum data needed to resume registry operations if the original registry cannot function and is unable or unwilling to transfer service gracefully. The data includes all objects related to registered domain names: the names themselves, contact information, and name servers.

The goal is higher resilience of registration services for the benefit of Internet users, both those registering information and those relying on the registry data. Domain name registries are required to escrow data as part of regulations for generic Top-Level Domains (gTLDs), and many country code TLD (ccTLD) managers and registrars also participate in data escrow.
sections.plainLanguage: A domain registry keeps a backup copy of all its domain records (who owns what, contact info, and name servers) with a trusted company. If something bad happens, that company has the records needed to restart the registry.

sections.title: Why Standardization Matters
sections.content:
In the past, almost every registry that used data escrow developed its own specification. As more domain registries came online and the number of TLDs grew, this fragmentation became increasingly problematic. Different escrow formats meant that each registry needed custom handling, and there was no easy way for a backup registry to restore another registry's data.

RFC 8909 solves this by providing a single, standardized specification that any registry can use. The format is designed to be independent of the specific objects being escrowed, making it flexible enough for domain registries while potentially useful for other types of registries. Specifications for individual object types (like domain-specific data) can reference this general framework.
sections.plainLanguage: Before, each company made up its own way to back up domain records. That made it hard for a backup company to restore data from different registries. This RFC creates one standard way everyone can use.

sections.title: Three Types of Deposits
sections.content:
RFC 8909 defines three kinds of deposits, each with a specific purpose:

Full Deposit: Contains the complete, current state of the registry database at a specific point in time (called the Timeline Watermark). This is a complete snapshot and is the baseline from which other deposits are measured.

Incremental Deposit: Contains only the changes (additions, modifications, deletions) that have occurred since the previous Full Deposit. When rebuilding a registry, you apply incremental deposits on top of the most recent full deposit.

Differential Deposit: Contains only the changes since the immediately previous deposit, whether that was a Full, Incremental, or Differential Deposit. Unlike incremental deposits, differential deposits refer to the previous deposit rather than only to the full deposit. All transactions since that previous point in time are included, so each differential contains a complete accounting.
sections.plainLanguage: A Full deposit is a complete photo of the database at one moment. An Incremental deposit shows only the changes since the last Full deposit. A Differential shows only what changed since the very last deposit of any type.

sections.title: The Deposit Format
sections.content:
Deposits are represented as XML documents containing a root <deposit> element. This element has required attributes: a type attribute (FULL, INCR, or DIFF), an id that uniquely identifies the deposit, and optionally a prevId that identifies the previous deposit (required for differential deposits, optional for incremental ones).

Inside the deposit element are child elements: a <watermark> element containing the date-time of the deposit's snapshot, and an <rdeMenu> element listing the version (which must be 1.0) and the namespaces of the objects being escrowed. The deposit also contains optional <deletes> and <contents> elements that hold the actual registry objects. Full deposits only have contents; incremental and differential deposits can have both.
sections.plainLanguage: A deposit is an XML document that says what type it is (complete, incremental, or changes-only), when it was made, what objects are included, and what was deleted or added.

sections.title: Rebuilding a Registry from Deposits
sections.content:
When applying incremental or differential deposits to rebuild a registry, the order matters because objects may depend on each other. The specification requires that all <deletes> sections be applied first in order, then all <contents> sections in order.

If an object appears in multiple deposits (for example, both a full deposit and a subsequent differential deposit), the version from the most recent deposit (as determined by the watermark timestamp) should be used. The specification also advises that an object should not appear multiple times within a single deposit's contents or deletes sections. When reconstructing from a full deposit, any deletes section must be ignored since a full deposit represents a complete state.
sections.plainLanguage: To rebuild a database: first erase everything marked for deletion, then add or update everything in the new deposit. Use the newest version if the same thing appears in multiple deposits.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The specification itself does not define how deposits are transmitted or secured; those mechanisms are the responsibility of implementations. However, the RFC emphasizes that depending on local policies, portions of a deposit may contain sensitive information, and parties should encrypt data at rest and in transit to prevent inadvertent disclosure.

Critically, authentication credentials MUST NOT be included in escrow deposits. Both the escrow agent must authenticate the registry before accepting deposits, and the registry must authenticate the escrow agent before submitting any data. The RFC also recommends that integrity-checking mechanisms be used to ensure data is transmitted correctly and that the contents are meaningful, and if TLS is used, the recommendations in RFC 7525 must be followed.
sections.plainLanguage: Keep the backups encrypted and secret. Don't back up passwords or secret keys. Make sure the registry and the backup company prove who they are to each other.
